content.thinking:
I'm planning out the monster truck's real-world proportions without being able to test it live, working through tire diameter, wheelbase, track width, and overall height to keep the model proportionally accurate.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy -- a chassis root joint with hinge joints for each wheel, plus separate steering joints for the front wheels so the truck can turn, making sure all the positions line up with the body and tire dimensions I just worked out.

For the tire geometry, I'm weighing options: a cylinder rotated to align with the wheel axis works for aiming, but texturing the tread is tricky since cylinder caps share the same UV mapping as the sides. Thinking through using a lathe shape with a cell-painted chevron tread pattern instead to avoid that distortion.

Working out the chevron tread algorithm based on quantized angle and height steps, with dark lug colors against gap colors for a pixel-art tire look, then sketching the lathe profile points to define the tire's cross-sectional shape.

Working out the lug pattern across the texture columns — trying 12 lugs at 30° spacing with chevron detail every 7.5°, figuring out the column indexing to alternate lug segments correctly.

Thinking about resolution: with tires roughly 0.36m per lug and paint texel density around 7mm per pixel at 1024px, bumping to 2048 or using a 4096 atlas would sharpen things, and I want pixelated sampling for the chevron/grille details rather than smoothing. For the chevron rows, I'm mapping height along the tire axis into discrete bands and mirroring them symmetrically, then shifting the column index per row to create a diagonal zigzag look.

I'm steepening the chevron shift to two columns per row for a sharper diagonal, then figuring out how to detect sidewalls versus tread using the axis-relative normal or height cutoff, and passing per-tire center coordinates into the paint function so I can compute radial distance for sidewall ring decorations like a lighter protector ring near the rim. I'm also considering whether to leave the tread flat with painted chevrons or add actual raised lug geometry for a more realistic silhouette, but leaning toward keeping it simpler with just painted detail for now.

Writing lug placement matrices...

Checking the lug box depth at 0.865 clears the floor margin fine, and even with the 25° tilt, the radial extension from the tilted corners stays small enough to stay within tolerance.

For paint, I'll simplify: keep the lathe tread itself dark with subtle sidewall details rather than double-painting chevrons, and let the lugs carry the geometric pattern distinction instead.

Now I'm adding sidewall tick marks using an angular calculation from the center point, quantized into alternating light/dark bands to suggest lettering, plus a ring detail near the shoulder. Then I'm sketching the wheel rim as a separate chrome cylinder with a blue center cap and lug nuts, sized to sit just outside the tire's radius.

Defining the rim's color bands by radial distance for a blue hub center, dark ring, dithered silver mid-section, and chrome edge, applied to the outer face of each wheel and cheaply mirrored on the inner disc.

I'm positioning the rim disc recessed into the tire for a deep-dish look, setting disc radius and thickness so the lip sits at the tire's inner bore edge, then placing matching discs on both the outer and inner sides of the hub.

For the lathe geometry, I'm orienting the axis along x so the wheel outline revolves correctly around the hub centerline. Now I'm thinking through the front axle housing between the wheels—positioning a connecting rod and differential pumpkin, and working out where the axle needs to sit relative to the hub placement at the wheel edges.

Steering joints will live at the axle height facing up with the wheel geometry parented underneath, aimed outward along x for left/right naming. I'm also planning the four-link suspension rods and coilover shocks running from the axle to the chassis rails, paired near the body like the reference, and considering a helical sweep for the spring geometry.

Building the coil spring geometry...

Writing cylinder helper geometry...

Now I'm sketching the pickup truck body's rough bounding dimensions: a boxy 1980s-style chassis with hood, cab, and bed sections stacked along the z-axis with different heights and widths for each part.

I'm working out the blue paint job with flame decals on the sides—defining a procedural flame shape using the surface normal and position to layer yellow, orange, and red tongues sweeping backward across the body.

Checking that the sweep direction works: since phase depends on u plus a fraction of v, increasing v pulls the constant-phase line toward lower u, so the tongue tips lean backward toward -z as intended. I'm layering the flame colors by threshold—outer yellow at the full envelope, then orange and red at progressively tighter thresholds for the inner glow.

Picking the specific hex values for flame tiers and body shading, then setting up a pixel-cell quantization scheme so each cell gets a flat color based on its center position and normal. Adding randomized amplitude variation per flame tongue so they don't look perfectly uniform.

I'm applying that same flame paint function across hood, doors, and bed sides for continuity, then reconsidering whether the body needs wheel arch cutouts -- since the tires sit below the body line here, arches may not be necessary unlike the reference image.

I'm rechecking the geometry: raising the body bottom to around 1.8 to avoid overlapping the tire tops, then considering whether to fake wheel-well darkening by painting dark arcs near the wheel centers where the body meets the tire radius.

Given the clearance works out, I'll add a thin dark arch outline as a cheap decorative fender flare, extruding a half-ring shape along the wheel area to suggest a wheel-well trim.

Writing extrusion coordinates...

The arch trim only clips into a tiny sliver of the body, so I'll drop it entirely — the truck just reads as a lifted vehicle with tire tops visible past the body from the side view, which works fine. Now I'm listing out the body details starting with the frame rails.

Adding the rocker and underbody chassis box, then building the hood as a nose-shaped box with blue flame paint, a raised hood scoop with a dark vented front face, and thin painted seam lines.

Now I'm positioning the front grille as a textured plane with a chrome-ish frame, plus flanking headlight squares sized and spaced symmetrically across the face width.

Also sketching smaller orange turn-signal panels below the headlights, using the glow kit so lights read as emissive, then adding a chrome bumper box with fog lamp slot texturing and a pair of red tow hooks.

Next I'm shaping the cab: lower body panels continuing from the hood, a tapered greenhouse above with slanted A-pillars, and a windshield plane angled by computing its outward-and-up normal vector so the glass tilts correctly between the beltline and roof.

Side windows get pixel-art glass textures with diagonal highlight streaks, roughly trapezoidal but approximated as rectangles with door-frame lines, mirrored symmetrically on both sides. I'm also considering whether to add interior details like seats, a dashboard, and steering wheel, but since the glass texture will likely be opaque dark, the interior probably won't be visible anyway.

For glass, I'll use mostly transparent pixel texture with a few opaque light-blue streak pixels so it reads as glass while staying see-through, framed by a dark window edge.

For the seats I'm planning dark grey boxes for base and back plus a headrest, a torus steering wheel tilted at the dash, and black roll cage rods including a visible rear roll bar arching from the cab roof to the bed.

Now I'm adding details like a light bar with four glowing light housings atop the roof, chrome side mirrors, door handles, and seam lines painted as thin dark strips along the body, plus setting up the bed floor height.

For the bed itself I'm defining the side walls, front wall, and tailgate as boxes, along with a darker rim cap, then thinking about what to populate the bed with -- maybe a silver toolbox near the cab, some extra tires, or other gear to give the truck more character.

I'm adding twin chrome exhaust stacks rising from the bed behind the cab, each with a flared top and glowing orange flame tips, plus glowing red taillight planes on the tailgate and a dark rear bumper with a pixel-art license plate reading "MONSTR".

Now I'm sketching a simple decal for the door, a pixel number plane facing outward on each side, making sure the orientation reads correctly from the viewer's perspective.

I'll also add a pinstripe accent below the window line, a power-bulge ridge on the hood, and skip extras like antenna or hitch for simplicity.

For the underbody I'm placing the drivetrain: driveshaft and differential pumpkins at the axles, four-link suspension bars connecting axle to frame, steering linkage, and panhard bar. I'm positioning shocks and coil springs near the frame rails, adjusting their x-offsets slightly so they clear the rail width without overlapping.

I'm nudging the shock positions inward so they don't collide with the tire's inner sidewall, then double-checking that the spring radius still clears the frame rail. Overall I'm verifying the truck's total height comes out around 3.6 meters and width across the tires near 3.76 meters, which lines up with a realistic full-size pickup scale.

Now I'm planning the joint hierarchy: steering hinges for the front wheels, standard wheel hinges for all four, plus hinge joints for the doors, tailgate, and hood. I'm working out where each hinge sits—door hinges along the front vertical edge, tailgate hinge at the rear bottom edge—and how each panel attaches as its own bone with the right axis orientation for rotation.

I'm also setting up a geometry-merging helper that buckets meshes by color so they can be flushed into single parts sharing the chassis bone, making sure all merged shapes use consistent indexed attributes. Then I'm defining a tight color palette (blues, chrome, steel, blacks, reds, yellows, tire rubber tones) to stay within the flat-color budget while keeping the paint colors separate from the count.

I'm calculating texel density across the painted surfaces -- body panels and tire sidewalls -- to settle on a texture sheet size (2048px) and cell size (around 4cm for body/tire, 2cm for fine details) so the pixel-art look stays consistent at that scale. Now I'm working out the cellPaint logic for the tire sidewalls, using radial distance from the cell center to quantize rings of color for the hub, tread, and lettering areas based on face normal and angle.

Writing the flame color ramp...

Still writing flame layer logic...

Since door parts share model-space coordinates with the body, the same seam positions should apply across both -- front seam around z=0.92-0.93 and rear around z=-0.3 to -0.32, with the hood/fender seam landing at roughly the same z value too, so a single seam rule can cover all of them.

I'm also planning a belt trim pinstripe around y=2.58-2.62 for the lower panel edge, then setting up helper functions to build boxes with chassis bone attachments, bucket geometries by color for merging, and using mergeGeometries from three.js addons to combine same-colored parts into single meshes before adding them.

I'm working out per-wheel bone merging with a map keyed by color and bone, plus a tube helper that builds a cylinder aimed between two points for connecting joints, and sketching out how to approximate coil springs using stacked thin cylinder discs along the spring axis.

For the shock absorber I'm planning a chrome shaft tube plus a darker body cylinder sized to roughly 40% of the shaft length, with the tire geometry built via a lathe shape and lug nuts merged into buckets painted on the wheel bone in local model space.

Now I'm working out wheel geometry per side: positioning the joint outward along x at the wheel bone, then building the rim as paired discs offset from center, a beadlock ring of fourteen small bolt boxes around the rim radius, a blue hub cylinder, and a chrome center cap with six nuts, all merged into appropriate color buckets.

I'm defining the paint pattern for the wheel face using radial distance bands -- blue near center, black ring, silver dithered zone, then a chrome beadlock region with angle-quantized bolt cells -- and checking that the tire's inner bore and recessed hub placement line up correctly before refining the tire sidewall bulge profile.

Now I'm plotting the sidewall outline points and tread lug box dimensions, making sure the lug protrusion height and radial centering keep the lowest point within tolerance, then adjusting tread width and chevron proportions for the lugs.

Recomputing the outer edge places it at roughly 0.315, which fits nicely within the 0.3-0.42 shoulder region where the lathe radius tapers from 0.84 down to 0.82. That geometry checks out, so now I'm thinking about distributing 18 lugs with a staggered pattern.

Each lug alternates its V-shape to point toward the direction of rotation, with 18 lugs on each side generating roughly 432 triangles per tire total. The tangential spacing works out fine too—circumference divided by lug count gives about 0.29, comfortably covering the 0.17 width plus tilt. I'm setting up the box geometry for each lug with rotation and translation transforms to position and tilt them correctly around the tire.

Now I'm defining pixel-art textures for the light components, using small 8x8 and 10x7 grids with palette colors like dark black, light yellow, and white to create headlight and light bar patterns.

Still writing textures...

For the interior, I should include seats, dash, steering wheel, and maybe a small driver figure visible through the windows—a simple head box with skin tone plus a red helmet for a fun monster-truck driver look.

Working out the cab geometry: positioning seats, seat backs, steering wheel on the driver's side (US-style left side), and sizing a torso box for the driver figure with the helmet and visor details.

Still laying out dimensions...

Still placing panels...

Adding pillar geometry and sizing the roof box, extending it slightly forward as a visor lip over the windshield.

Now I'm computing the windshield plane's angled vector and normal, setting its width and height, and positioning pillars at each end. Then I'm placing a light bar housing centered on the roof top.

Positioning the four individual light boxes across the bar and adding a glow plane in front, then starting on the roll bar tubes rising behind the cab and sloping back above roof level.

Now I'm sketching the roll bar's curved tube paths, crossbars, and diagonal braces, plus chrome exhaust stacks behind the cab with flared tops and glowing orange flame spikes. I'm also laying out the truck bed floor and side wall boxes with the body paint and flame pattern extending onto them.

I'm designing the hinged tailgate as a separate box joint with its own paint rules, considering embossed panel lines and a simple pixel-art emblem (a lightning bolt motif) for the rear panel, plus adding chrome bed rail caps and thinking about small bed accessories like a toolbox or spare tire.

For the bed decor, I'm placing nitrous bottles with chrome/red-top cylinders, a small cooler with a white lid, and a checkered racing flag on a pole at the rear corner, working out how to orient the flag using two opposite-facing planes so it reads correctly from both sides.

Now I'm shifting to the car's nose section, sizing the front box and hood: a lower hood body, a slightly raised and inset hood top plate for a fender-step look, and a hood scoop box positioned near the front.

Working out the front face details: dark intake slats, grille and headlight placement with paired stacked headlights and amber signal lights below, plus chrome surround framing for the grille, all positioned relative to the nose box's front plane at z=2.2.

Now I'm adding the bumper geometry with metallic paint, dark intake slots, red tow hooks, and a dark push bar made of tube rods bracing the front. I'm also sketching out side mirrors as small chrome boxes mounted on arm rods near the A-pillar.

Thinking through remaining details, I decide to skip wipers, mud flaps, and most underbody mechanical parts since they're mostly hidden from typical hero camera angles, though I note the front axle could use a tie rod and drag link for realism.

Adding drive axle shafts, differential housing, and axle stubs connecting to the wheel hubs...

Then I'm placing the planetary hub cylinder, brake rotor, and caliper on each wheel bone, confirming the joint count comes to ten with root, steering, wheel, door, tailgate and hood joints. I'm working out the hood joint's hinge position and aim direction, then positioning the door parts — box, chrome sill trim, handle, and mirror — relative to the door joint, and sizing the door body panel to fit the door opening dimensions.

Now I'm aligning the outer x-plane of the nose, doors, and bed walls so they share the same 0.98 edge without z-fighting, while checking the door and nose panels only touch at their boundary. I'm sizing and placing the number decal on the door as a small textured plane with a dark circle and white numeral, making sure the flame paint pattern sits beneath it and stays within the door's vertical bounds. I'm also capping the flame pattern's height so it doesn't bleed onto the roof's thin side faces.

I want to add subtle mud-splatter speckling near the lower body using per-cell randomness, darkening cells below a certain height with a probability that increases toward the sill. Now I'm starting to write the actual TypeScript module, importing geometry merging utilities, the path builder, and math helpers to begin constructing the truck model.

Setting up imports and types...

Adding box and tube helpers, then merging all accumulated geometries by color and bone before finalizing parts, double-checking that indexed geometries like cylinders, toruses, and spheres merge cleanly.

Now I'm designing the paint logic for the body, using a hash function and color ramps to generate flame-like patterns along the car's sides based on vertical position and door seam boundaries.

Writing flame paint pattern logic...

Below that, I'm adding mud splatter near the car's underside with a brownish palette, then falling back to the blue ramp for the rest of the body, shading based on surface normal and face axis to approximate ambient lighting with slight random dithering.

I want to tone down the top brightness a bit, using a softer blend factor. I'm also adding a dark sill stripe along the lower side panel before the mud layer kicks in, so the two effects can overlap naturally. Now I'm starting the tire paint function, which measures distance from a wheel's center axis to carve out the tire ring and begin mapping tread detail around its circumference.

Writing tire tread logic...

Writing wheel rim shading logic...

Designing pixel art textures...

Writing grille texture logic...

Still writing texture generators...

Still designing pixel sprites...

Now I'm working out the orientation for the rear face at (0, 2.35, -2.36), facing -Z, computing the local right axis via cross product so the viewer standing behind sees it correctly oriented.

I'm placing a license plate on the tailgate: a light gray plate with dark pseudo-letter blocks and a border, sized 0.36x0.18, positioned below the emblem and above the tail lights, which sit at x = ±0.78.

Now I'm computing the exact z-position for the tail lights against the tailgate's rear face, accounting for box thickness, and widening the tail light spacing to x = ±0.74 to match the bed's inner wall width of 1.76. I'm also laying out the rear bumper as a chrome-painted box positioned below the tailgate, and sketching in the frame rails as long boxes running along the underside at x = ±0.4.

Now I'm adding crossmembers along the frame at several z-positions, a dark underbody pan to fill the gap between the rails and the body floor, and planning the nose box dimensions while nudging its z-span to avoid overlapping the door panel's edge. I'm also starting to spec out the hood plate as a separate painted body part.

Continuing on, I'm sizing the hood scoop with its vent plane, the cab rear wall positioned behind the door, and small pillar boxes above it for structure. I'm listing out the remaining body parts still needed: roof box, A-pillar rods, door boxes, and the bed walls with tailgate.

Still planning geometry...

I'm checking that the roof crossbar and exhaust stacks don't actually collide, adjusting the stack heights slightly for clearance, then moving on to building the front axle assembly — a dark tube housing between the wheel hubs with a spherical differential pumpkin positioned at the axle centerline.

Still writing suspension layout...

Still placing underbody parts...

I'll add small U-joints and slightly sloped driveshaft rods, then consider whether to place a fuel cell box under the bed without conflicting with the rear axle area.

Now I'm working out the wheel assembly: lathing the tire profile around each wheel bone, merging lug nuts into a dark bucket geometry, and adding rim discs as cylinders oriented along the axle direction with proper paint and positioning on both sides.

I'm also laying out hub bolts in a ring pattern, placing the hub cylinder and chrome cap, positioning six lug nuts in a tighter radius, and computing bolt coordinates in the YZ plane so I can finish with the steel stub axle extending inward from the wheel center.

I realize the brake rotor and caliper would actually be hidden inside the enclosed rim discs, so I decide to skip rendering them entirely, while making sure the stub axle still reaches the housing without leaving a visible gap between tire and axle.

Checking the tire geometry, the tread bottom sits just above the floor so it's touching correctly, and overall x-bounds come out to ±1.87 which looks right. Now I'm starting on the door components — the panel box attached to the door bone, plus a chrome window sill strip.

Continuing with door details: adding the handle box, a separate number decal plane positioned away from the handle, and a side mirror assembly with an arm, chrome housing, and small glass box mounted near the A-pillar. I'm also placing the window glass plane on the chassis bone sized to the door opening, and starting on the window frame trim along the roofline.

For the rear window I'm sizing a plane to fit between the rear pillars with its own pixel texture, and planning dedicated textures for front and side glass panels sized to roughly match their aspect ratios so the interior (dash, seats, driver, roll cage) is visible through them from outside.

Now I'm building the driver figure: a torso box positioned on the seat base, a head/skin box, and a red helmet box with a dark visor plane, all sized and placed relative to the seat and roof height so the figure sits naturally inside the cabin.

For the steering wheel, I'm computing the torus rotation so its default face normal (pointing along z) gets tilted toward the driver using trigonometry on the rotation angle.

Then I'm working out the steering column and arm placements connecting dash to wheel, plus skipping an antenna detail, and figuring out the light bar housings along the roof — four evenly spaced boxes with glowing light panels in front.

I'm deciding to skip the sun visor and fog lights to keep the bumper texture unlit rather than glowing, since glow would also light up the dark parts of the texture. For the bed, I'm placing nitro bottle tubes on either side near the tailgate and considering where to fit a cooler without clashing with them.

I'm settling on a cooler with a red body and light lid positioned centrally in the bed, skipping the spare tire idea but adding a coiled tow chain as a flattened torus tucked into a bucket shape. I'm also adding small tie-down loop boxes along the bed rails, and deciding against hood flames or pinstripes to keep the paint simple on just the sides.

Setting up imports and utility functions for the build...

Writing the build function...

I'm noticing a potential issue: the wheel joint sits at the exact same position as its steering parent joint, which could create a zero-length bone and cause problems in aim calculations. I should offset the kingpin joint slightly to avoid this degenerate case.

Adding a texture-plane decal helper...

I'm checking that paint and color types line up for the body part helper, then writing a cylinder helper for struts before building a shock/spring generator that places alternating cylinder segments along a line and wraps them with a steel tube.

Writing tire lug geometry...

Working out chevron symmetry so both sides mirror correctly, then adding sidewall shoulder knob boxes to round out the tire silhouette. Now I'm setting up the full color palette as named constants to reuse across all the tire and vehicle parts before writing the complete file.

Writing glass texture pattern...

Still designing the plate texture...

Still writing bumper texture...

Now I'm working out the front face geometry, positioning the grille surround and plane against the nose face so they sit flush within its bounds, then placing headlight surrounds at corresponding z coordinates.

I notice the grille and headlight x-ranges overlap, so I'm narrowing the grille width and shifting it inward to clear the headlight span, adjusting the headlight tex plane size to match.

I'm then checking vertical overlap between the amber indicators, headlights, and bumper box — the bumper top edge clips into the amber lights, so I'm recalculating the bumper's y-center and height to sit lower, and nudging the amber indicator's y-position upward with its surround so everything stays within the nose face bounds without clipping.

I'm continuing to adjust the push-bar/brush-guard rods in front of the grille — placing vertical tubes at x ±0.55 running from the bumper up past the grille, plus a horizontal cross-bar, while making sure the whole assembly stays within the front z-bound of 2.5.

Now I'm moving on to finish out the body: using frame paint for the underpan and rails, adding door handles, and building the roof as a box above z -0.35..0.75 so the windshield top lines up at z 0.66. Then I start defining the rod pillars...

Still writing pillar geometry...

Now I'm planning the remaining parts -- rear pillar boxes, window plane sizing, glow intensity on the light bar, headlights, amber markers and taillights, plus hood components (plate, scoop, vent) attached to the hood bone, and a cooler assembly with a red body and white lid. I need to double-check the type signatures, especially that `at` accepts readonly number arrays for positions, before writing the actual code.

Now I'm sketching out the frame hoops and cross braces using sweep and rod helpers with dark chrome coloring, then finishing with the chassis return statement. I'm also working out the flag pole and flag plane placement at the rear bumper, making sure the flag orientation and attachment side line up correctly with the pole position. I estimate the part count will land around a hundred pieces across roughly forty merged buckets, and I'm skipping extra wheel well detail to keep things simple, while making sure every constant I declare actually gets used to satisfy strict TypeScript settings before I start writing the final file.
